A1.notes.Q3: Course grades are essential for me as an advisor to understand academic progress, so moderate gain is acceptable. Admissions data helps context but feels too far removed from daily study struggles; I'm hesitant without a clear trigger.

A2.notes.Q3: Credits + grades are baseline for us, so small improvement is okay to catch edge cases. High school data predicts risk well (large threshold). Absalon clicks feel invasive; need moderate gain. Age/gender don't add safety info but privacy concerns outweigh benefit unless fairness improves.
A2.notes.Q4: Trust is critical when advising students personally. 'High' explainability might miss a few at-risk kids, but we can't work with black boxes in a supportive role.
A2.notes.Q5: We cannot accept bias if it harms marginalized groups disproportionately. Losing up to 3 overall hits is acceptable to ensure equity, but both recall and false positives must be balanced for genuine help.
A2.notes.Q6: Students don't know their struggles until they hit a wall. Waiting for explicit request often means too late; personalized messages are effective and timely.
A2.notes.Q7: With generic emails, mass notification is okay to deter students from hiding. With personalized advice, false positives waste precious advisor time and damage trust; selectivity should increase.

A3.notes.Q3: I worry about surveillance, especially with behavior tracking like Absalon page views, which feels invasive compared to grades or credits alone.
A3.notes.Q4: As an advisor, I need to be able to explain *why* a student is struggling so they trust the feedback and actually engage with support.
A3.notes.Q5: We shouldn't miss false positives; flagging students who are doing fine damages their reputation more than missing a rare case of real struggle if we can catch the common ones.
A3.notes.Q6: I think support must be immediate when risks appear, but keep it low-stigma by starting with generic info before escalating.
A3.notes.Q7: With personalized emails, the consequence of misidentifying someone is higher due to stigma, so being slightly more selective feels safer than casting a wide net.
A3.Q8.1: I'm concerned about algorithmic bias where our model reinforces stereotypes about certain demographics rather than learning individual progress patterns.

S2.notes.Q3: As a working student from outside the EU, I worry about surveillance. Grades are okay for me since I know how they affect my degree. But Absalon data feels invasive; no one checks if I'm logged in unless something goes wrong.
S2.notes.Q5: Missing students because the model favors another group is worse than contacting a few extra people who might not need help right now. We can't afford to let certain groups fall through.
S2.notes.Q6: I shouldn't have to wait until next year or semester for help if the model sees I'm struggling now, regardless of when it flags me.
S2.notes.Q7: Personalized messages hit harder and can be annoying if I'm working late or don't need support yet. Balance is better to avoid harassment while still reaching out.
S2.Q8.1: The model could miss me being in a mental health crisis just because of grades, ignoring my actual struggle with burnout vs low ability.

S3.notes.Q3: Standard academic data is okay if it helps me get support, but invasive bio-data like race or nationality feels wrong given the Danish context. Disability status must be included because of my own experience.
S3.notes.Q4: I need to understand exactly why I'm being flagged so an advisor can help me specifically. Black boxes are terrifying for someone navigating health hurdles.
S3.notes.Q5: It's unfair if the model systematically misses people like me from marginalized backgrounds. Fairness isn't just about numbers; it's about equity in getting help when I need it most.
S3.notes.Q6: Health issues flare up suddenly. I'd prefer proactive support over waiting for me to explicitly request help annually.
S3.notes.Q7: With personalized messages, privacy is more at risk, so minimizing unnecessary contact outweighs the benefit of catching a few missed cases in my specific case.
S3.Q8.1: I worry that even good intentions with predictive models might lead to labeling and reduced trust between students and staff once 'data' decides their struggles for them rather than empathy doing it first.

S4.notes.Q3: Course performance is useful context but shouldn't be invasive. Disability data must have a high threshold because I am it; other sensitive groups need significant proof of benefit.
S4.notes.Q4: As a student advisor, I believe students need to know why they are flagged to feel heard. Very low explainability feels like surveillance without recourse.
S4.notes.Q5: We shouldn't disproportionately flag or assume difficulties for marginalized groups (e.g., ADHD students). Preventing false positives is crucial to avoid stigma.
S4.notes.Q6: Early detection saves lives and studies for me. Waiting until a warning is issued too late; continuous monitoring allows timely adjustments.
S4.notes.Q7: Generic emails feel like spam to non-students, wasting resources. Personalized outreach has higher stakes but also risks of unnecessary stress if done indiscriminately.
S4.Q8.1: I worry that the model will over-identify ADHD students due to missed deadlines and missing page views in Absalon before I even realize what's happening.

S5.notes.Q3: I feel very hesitant about using online activity data like page views from Absalon. It feels invasive and might make me self-conscious while studying, especially since I'm already adjusting to the Danish system.

S6.notes.Q3: I trust the disability data since it directly affects my experience, but age/gender/race feel too invasive for a law student from abroad.
S6.notes.Q4: I want to know why I'm flagged, but if the rule is very complex (like AI), it might miss me as a non-native speaker who struggles with language.
S6.notes.Q5: Fairness matters more to me than catching everyone; I don't want false alarms that annoy people unnecessarily.
S6.notes.Q6: I need help immediately if my grades drop, so I prefer being contacted rather than waiting for a yearly check.
S6.notes.Q7: General emails are fine in bulk to save resources; personalized ones feel intrusive and can be ignored.

S8.Q8.1: (Free text field, left empty per instructions)

S9.notes.Q3: Grades matter a lot to me, but I worry about Absalon activity data feeling like surveillance. If it catches real struggles early (5 more students), that small cost is worth the peace of mind.
S9.notes.Q4: I trust simple rules more because they are fair and understandable, but complex models could catch nuances like burnout that grades miss.
